paragraphs: The paper studies how to estimate precision matrices in Gaussian graphical models under M-matrix constraints, including the more restrictive diagonally dominant case. The estimation task involves both recovering the matrix and identifying graph edges, so the authors assess their method on both outcomes.

These constrained models have an unusual property: a maximum likelihood estimate can exist with very few observations. The abstract states that two observations can suffice for M-matrices, and even one can suffice for diagonally dominant M-matrices. This concerns the existence of an estimate; it does not establish that such tiny samples yield accurate recovery.

The proposed method improves its estimate through multiple adaptive stages. Each stage solves a weighted ℓ1-regularized problem. To carry out these steps, the authors develop a shared gradient projection framework, using different projections to accommodate the two kinds of matrix constraints.

The authors provide theoretical analysis of estimation error and evaluate the method on synthetic and financial time-series datasets. They report better precision-matrix estimation and graph-edge identification than state-of-the-art methods in those evaluations. Together, these contributions address how to compute constrained estimates and how well the resulting estimates perform.
icml-2023-adaptive-estimation-of-graphic.tldr: An adaptive multistage method estimates constrained Gaussian graphical models, with theoretical error analysis and reported empirical improvements in matrix estimation and graph-edge identification.

paragraphs: This paper examines a threat in which an attacker slightly changes a neural network’s parameters. Earlier parameter attacks can expose themselves by making the network noticeably worse on ordinary inputs. The proposed adversarial parameter attack instead aims to preserve ordinary accuracy while substantially weakening resistance to adversarial examples.

The distinction matters because a network can appear to function normally on standard samples while becoming much easier to attack with carefully perturbed inputs. The paper therefore separates two properties that routine accuracy checks might conflate: correct predictions on ordinary data and robustness when inputs are adversarially manipulated.

Under stated reasonable conditions, the authors prove that nearly perfect adversarial parameters exist for perturbations measured using the L∞ and L0 norms. They also provide algorithms and evaluate attacks on commonly used networks trained with various robustness methods. Across the adversarial evaluation methods considered, attacked networks lose substantial robustness. These results support a conditional theoretical vulnerability and an empirical concern about robustness surviving small changes to model parameters.
icml-2023-adversarial-parameter-attack-o.tldr: Small parameter changes can leave ordinary accuracy largely intact while substantially weakening a network’s adversarial robustness.

paragraphs: Object-centric representation learning organizes visual information around objects and has been proposed as useful preparation for reinforcement learning from images. However, much of its evaluation has focused on indirect measures, such as segmentation quality or predicting object properties. Those measures do not directly establish whether the representations help an agent learn to act.

This paper investigates that connection through reinforcement-learning experiments. The authors introduce a simple visual benchmark organized around objects and use it to examine whether object-centric pretraining improves task performance and helps generalization outside the training distribution. This shifts evaluation toward the downstream decisions that the representation is intended to support.

The study also examines visually complex environments and the choice of pooling layer used to combine separate object representations. Its findings provide empirical insights into both usefulness and potential limitations in particular scenarios. The abstract does not establish a universal benefit; its contribution is a systematic examination of when object-centric pretraining helps and which integration choices deserve attention.
icml-2023-an-investigation-into-pre-trai.tldr: A systematic empirical study examines the benefits, limits, and integration choices of object-centric pretraining for visual reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Quantum neural networks combine parameterized quantum operations with classical optimization for tasks such as supervised learning. Understanding how their training converges remains difficult. One approach borrows tangent-kernel analysis from classical neural networks, using a kernel derived at initialization to describe subsequent learning.

This paper shows that quantum-network training has behavior that such kernel regression cannot capture. The authors connect the discrepancy to the unitarity of quantum operations and identify a non-negligible departure from the tangent-kernel description at random initialization. For networks using Pauli measurements, they prove convergence is at most sublinear, a result beyond the explanatory reach of the kernel-regression dynamics considered.

The authors then characterize the actual dynamics in the limit of overparameterization. Their description accounts for changes in convergence rate during training and indicates that the range of measurements is crucial for fast convergence. The contribution is therefore a different theoretical account of quantum-network learning, with measurement choices playing a central role in the resulting training behavior.
icml-2023-analyzing-convergence-in-quant.tldr: Quantum neural-network dynamics depart from tangent-kernel regression, with measurement ranges crucial to convergence speed.

paragraphs: Training-data extraction attempts to recover material used to train a language model and can help assess privacy leakage. The paper starts from the observation that many existing extraction methods remain demonstrations of possibility rather than especially effective evaluation tools. It investigates practical choices that can make these methods more capable.

The study follows a common two-stage process: generate text that might belong to the training data, then rank those candidates using criteria intended to identify likely matches. It benchmarks choices in both stages on a publicly available dataset. These include sampling strategies for generation and token-level criteria for ranking, keeping attention on how the overall extraction pipeline behaves.

Experiments with GPT-Neo 1.3B show that several previously overlooked choices can be crucial to extraction success. The proposed collection of tricks substantially improves over the baseline in most evaluated cases. The result supplies a stronger reference point for future extraction research and shows why assessing privacy leakage depends partly on the effectiveness of the extraction procedure.
icml-2023-bag-of-tricks-for-training-dat.tldr: Benchmarking generation and ranking choices produces a stronger training-data extraction baseline for GPT-Neo 1.3B.

paragraphs: Graph classification often requires many task-specific labels, which can be expensive to obtain. This paper considers using labeled graphs from another domain to support learning in an unlabeled target domain. Two central obstacles are capturing enough information about graph structure and handling differences between the source and target domains.

CoCo addresses both through two coupled learning branches. A graph convolutional branch captures topology implicitly, while a hierarchical graph kernel branch captures it explicitly. A multi-view contrastive learning framework brings these complementary representations together, allowing the model to learn from different views of the same structural information.

The framework also encourages cross-domain examples with the same semantics to have similar representations. This connects richer structural understanding with the goal of aligning domains, rather than treating those objectives separately. Across experiments on popular datasets and different settings, CoCo generally outperforms the competing baselines. The findings support the usefulness of combining complementary graph views with semantic alignment for the domain-adaptation problems evaluated.
icml-2023-coco-a-coupled-contrastive-fra.tldr: CoCo combines complementary graph representations and cross-domain contrastive learning to improve classification in unlabeled target domains.

paragraphs: Code language models can synthesize programs, but their ability to reproduce licensed code raises intellectual-property concerns. CodeIPPrompt provides an automated platform for evaluating the extent of that reproduction. The paper treats systematic assessment as a necessary part of understanding a problem that has received comparatively limited attention.

The platform combines prompts built from a database of licensed code with a measurement tool for assessing generated outputs. These components link attempts to elicit licensed material with a consistent way to evaluate the resulting reproduction. The authors apply the platform to both open-source code models and commercial products.

The study reports IP violations across all models evaluated and attributes the problem to substantial amounts of restrictively licensed material in training corpora, arising from intentional inclusion and inconsistent licensing practices. It also explores fine-tuning and dynamic token filtering as possible mitigations. The stated outcome is a testbed for assessing these issues and evidence that better mitigation is needed, rather than a claim that the explored strategies solve the problem.
icml-2023-codeipprompt-intellectual-prop.tldr: CodeIPPrompt evaluates licensed-code reproduction in code models and reports widespread issues across the systems tested.

paragraphs: Error-correcting output codes can help neural networks withstand defects in the hardware running them. Existing approaches, however, can improve accuracy under defects while reducing accuracy on functioning hardware. Stronger codes also do not necessarily improve either measure. This paper connects these problems to correlation among errors.

COLA aims to reduce that correlation at several levels. Its architecture separates the final portions of paths leading to output nodes. It also orthogonalizes weights in shared layers to encourage orthogonal intermediate features. A further regularization term, based on total correlation, addresses dependence among errors at the outputs. Together, these changes coordinate network learning with the error-correction mechanism.

The authors provide theoretical analysis and experimental evaluation. They report improvements of up to 6.7% in clean accuracy over the original networks and up to 40% in robust accuracy over state-of-the-art code-enhanced networks. These are reported maximum improvements with different comparison points. The results support error decorrelation as a useful design principle for neural inference exposed to hardware defects.
icml-2023-cola-orchestrating-error-codin.tldr: COLA reduces correlated network errors to improve the effectiveness of error-correcting codes against hardware defects.

paragraphs: This paper studies continual-learning models as sources of pretrained representations for later tasks. Its evaluation asks how well the models support subsequent fine-tuning as they keep learning. In both supervised and unsupervised settings, the authors observe that transfer quality gradually improves rather than showing a noticeable decline.

They explain this pattern through a distinction between task-specific knowledge and features useful across tasks. A model may forget details of earlier tasks while developing representations that transfer better. Building on this observation, the paper proposes an unsupervised continual-learning framework based on masked modeling, intended to capture representations that remain useful across changing tasks.

The authors also introduce GLobal Attention Discretization, or GLAD, a fine-tuning scheme designed to preserve these general representations while adapting to a downstream task. Models fine-tuned with GLAD achieve competitive performance and remain useful as pretrained models themselves. The findings motivate a sustainable sequence of learning and adaptation, although the broader vision of continual improvement is presented as the authors’ interpretation rather than a universal guarantee.
icml-2023-continual-learners-are-increme.tldr: Continual learners can improve transferable representations even while forgetting task-specific knowledge, motivating methods that preserve general features.

paragraphs: Detecting incorrect training labels is an important part of learning from noisy data. Many approaches assume that no labels can be trusted as clean. This paper changes that setup by assuming access to a small clean subset, then investigates how that trusted information can improve detection throughout the training data.

The authors formulate detection as a multiple hypothesis testing problem. This makes the task one of evaluating many candidate label problems together, with attention to erroneous discoveries. Their method, BHN, incorporates the Benjamini-Hochberg procedure into deep neural networks, connecting a statistical testing approach with learned representations.

On CIFAR-10, the paper reports state-of-the-art performance and improvements over baselines of 28.48% in false discovery rate and 18.99% in F1. Ablation studies provide further support for the approach. The important qualification is that the method uses the assumed clean subset: its results demonstrate the value of that additional trusted evidence, rather than showing the same gains when all available labels are potentially unreliable.
icml-2023-delving-into-noisy-label-detec.tldr: BHN uses a small clean data subset and multiple hypothesis testing to improve noisy-label detection.

paragraphs: Active learning selects which unlabeled examples should receive labels next. This paper approaches that choice by looking for examples that could become important support vectors in a sparse kernel max-margin predictor. It uses the predictor’s dual representation to connect sample selection with the geometry of the learned decision boundary.

The authors derive upper and lower bounds on changes in the dual-form hinge loss. Those bounds motivate class-wise evidence scores formed from dual variables and kernel evaluations. A discovery function favors examples with little total evidence across classes, supporting exploration. A separate ranking function targets conflicting regions near the current decision boundary, supporting its refinement.

The two functions are automatically organized into successive phases: first discovering useful areas of the data, then ranking examples to improve the boundary. This provides a structured way to balance exploration with exploitation within one sampling process. Experiments on multiple real-world datasets report state-of-the-art active-learning performance, supporting the proposed connection between dual-space analysis and practical choices about which labels to acquire.
icml-2023-discover-then-rank-unlabeled-s.tldr: A two-phase active-learning strategy first discovers low-evidence samples, then targets conflicting regions to refine classification boundaries.

paragraphs: This paper studies agents that repeatedly choose among actions while collaborating through a communication network. An oblivious adversary assigns losses across both time and agents, so two agents choosing the same action simultaneously can receive different feedback. Each agent aims to compete with the single action that would have minimized cumulative loss averaged across the entire group.

That shared objective makes communication necessary: one agent’s observations do not directly reveal how an action performs for everyone. The authors establish lower bounds on achievable regret for settings with full-information feedback and settings where agents observe only feedback for their selected actions. These bounds characterize unavoidable difficulty in the problem.

For bandit feedback, the paper introduces FEDEXP3, a near-optimal algorithm. It guarantees sublinear regret without agents exchanging sequences of chosen-action identities or losses, answering an existing open question. Sublinear regret means the average performance gap to the hindsight benchmark diminishes over time. Numerical evaluations on synthetic and real-world datasets support the theoretical results and demonstrate effectiveness in the tested settings.
icml-2023-doubly-adversarial-federated-b.tldr: FEDEXP3 achieves near-optimal federated bandit learning when losses vary across agents and time without exchanging action or loss sequences.

paragraphs: The Hamiltonian matrix is an important prediction target in quantum chemistry and condensed matter physics. A network predicting it should respect the relevant spatial symmetries, but enforcing those symmetries can make computation expensive. This paper introduces QHNet to address efficiency and SE(3) equivariance within the same architecture.

QHNet’s design reduces the number of tensor products by 92% while retaining the required symmetry behavior. It also prevents the channel dimension from growing exponentially as additional atom types are included. These changes address computational costs inside the architecture, making the representation of physical structure less demanding without abandoning equivariance.

Experiments cover four molecular systems from the MD17 datasets. The authors report performance comparable to state-of-the-art methods at substantially greater speed, along with 50% lower memory consumption from the streamlined architecture. The stated result is therefore an efficiency improvement while maintaining comparable predictive performance in those evaluations. It demonstrates that the architectural cost of symmetry-respecting Hamiltonian prediction can be reduced substantially.
icml-2023-efficient-and-equivariant-grap.tldr: QHNet makes symmetry-respecting Hamiltonian prediction faster and less memory-intensive while achieving comparable performance on four tested molecular systems.

paragraphs: Supervised sequence learning provides both an input sequence and a desired output during training. EM-Network uses that target information to create compact oracle guidance representing context from the output side. With access to this guidance, the network makes better predictions than a model relying only on the source input.

The central challenge is passing that advantage to the original sequence model. The paper introduces a one-stage self-distillation strategy through which the model learns from EM-Network’s stronger predictions. This makes target-derived guidance a way to improve training, with knowledge transferred into the sequence model rather than leaving the benefit confined to the guided network.

The authors evaluate the approach with connectionist temporal classification models for speech recognition and attention-based encoder-decoder models for machine translation. They report improvements over the best prior speech-recognition work and state-of-the-art results on WMT’14 and IWSLT’14. These findings support the usefulness of oracle-guided self-distillation across the two different sequence-modeling settings examined.
icml-2023-em-network-oracle-guided-self-.tldr: EM-Network transfers the benefits of target-derived oracle guidance into sequence models through one-stage self-distillation.

paragraphs: End-to-end object detectors simplify prediction by eliminating hand-designed steps such as non-maximum suppression. Their training can nevertheless retain substantial heuristic machinery. This paper argues that those training choices can undermine the reliability of confidence scores and proposes a more compact probabilistic formulation of multi-object detection.

D-RMM treats the ground-truth bounding boxes as data whose density should be modeled by a regularized mixture. Training uses only two terms: negative log-likelihood and a regularizer called maximum component maximization. The likelihood term fits the observed boxes, while the regularizer is designed to prevent duplicate predictions. Together, they connect the detection objective with an explicit model of the box distribution.

The authors report that this formulation reduces training heuristics and improves confidence-score reliability. D-RMM also outperforms previous end-to-end detectors on MS COCO in the reported evaluation. The contribution concerns both the organization of training and its resulting predictions: a simpler objective supports competitive detection while addressing duplication and the trustworthiness of predicted confidence.
icml-2023-end-to-end-multi-object-detect.tldr: D-RMM trains object detection as regularized density estimation, reducing heuristics while improving confidence reliability and reported detection performance.

paragraphs: This paper learns compact video representations as keypoints without labeled supervision. Its starting idea is that the information within local pixel neighborhoods, and how that information evolves over time, can supply a training signal. Image spatial entropy provides the measure used to identify informative visual content.

The model is guided by two losses computed from local entropy. One encourages keypoints to cover spatial information in each frame. The other optimizes how keypoints carry information through time. This pairs a requirement to represent informative image regions with a requirement for temporal consistency, rather than learning isolated locations independently in each frame.

The authors evaluate the resulting representations on downstream tasks, including learning object dynamics, and report better performance than strong baselines. They also report handling static and moving objects, as well as objects that abruptly enter or leave a scene. These findings support local information content as a useful source of unsupervised guidance for learning keypoints that remain meaningful across changing video frames.
icml-2023-entropy-driven-unsupervised-ke.tldr: Two entropy-based objectives learn informative, temporally consistent video keypoints without labeled supervision.

paragraphs: Graph-neural-network research needs challenging datasets, but many large real-world graphs come from systems with strong privacy restrictions. This limits access and encourages repeated reliance on a small collection of public benchmarks. The paper proposes generating synthetic substitutes that retain useful characteristics for evaluating graph models.

The Computation Graph Transformer, or CGT, learns and reproduces real-world graph distributions with privacy control. Its objectives include processing large graphs and producing benchmarks on which graph neural networks perform similarly to how they perform on the source data. It incorporates existing privacy modules to provide end-user privacy guarantees for the generated graphs.

The authors compare CGT with a broad collection of graph-generative models. Within those experiments, they report that only CGT successfully combines large-scale generation, privacy control, and effective substitution for real-world benchmarking. The important outcome is not simply generating plausible graphs: it is preserving their usefulness as tests of graph-neural-network performance while addressing the privacy constraints that restrict access to the originals.
icml-2023-graph-generative-model-for-ben.tldr: CGT generates privacy-controlled synthetic graphs that preserve useful graph-neural-network benchmarking behavior at large scale.

paragraphs: Visual prompt tuning adapts a pretrained vision transformer by learning extra tokens while keeping the pretrained model frozen. Although effective with supervised pretraining, it often performs less well with self-supervised models. This paper investigates whether the problem depends on which transformer blocks interact with the prompts.

For MAE and MoCo v3 image classification, the authors observe better performance when prompts enter later blocks instead of the first block. This suggests that prompt placement matters and that an effective location may vary across models and tasks. Manually identifying the best placement for every future setting would be costly.

The proposed method learns a gate for each block to regulate its interaction with prompt tokens. These gates allow selective influence from blocks relevant to task adaptation, turning a placement decision into something learned during tuning. The method outperforms VPT variants on FGVC and VTAB classification and ADE20K semantic segmentation. The results support controlling where prompts interact with the model as an important part of adapting self-supervised transformers.
icml-2023-improving-visual-prompt-tuning.tldr: Learned block-level gates improve visual prompt tuning by controlling how prompts interact with self-supervised vision transformers.

paragraphs: This paper addresses generating musical soundtracks that follow rhythmic cues in a video. Existing approaches can be constrained by predefined music representations, while methods that directly generate waveforms have faced short outputs, limited application settings, and unstable quality. LORIS aims to support longer waveform generation conditioned on visual content.

The framework uses a latent conditional diffusion model for waveform synthesis. Context-aware conditioning encoders incorporate temporal information to support generation over longer spans. This makes the evolving video context part of the generation process. The authors also extend the application settings beyond dance to sports, including floor exercise and figure skating.

Alongside the model, the paper introduces a benchmark with preprocessed data, improved evaluation metrics, and generative baselines. Experiments report state-of-the-art musical quality and rhythmic correspondence for long-term soundtracks. These results address two connected requirements: producing convincing music and matching the visual rhythm. The benchmark provides a shared basis for evaluating both aspects of the soundtrack-generation problem.
icml-2023-long-term-rhythmic-video-sound.tldr: LORIS uses temporally conditioned diffusion to generate long musical soundtracks aligned with rhythmic video cues.

paragraphs: GAN training is commonly described as a discriminator estimating a divergence and a generator minimizing it. This paper argues that this explanation does not consistently match practical adversarial-training algorithms. It instead studies how generated samples move through sample space using Wasserstein gradient flows.

The proposed MonoFlow framework rescales particle evolution through a monotonically increasing transformation of the log density ratio. In this view, discriminator training supplies a vector field describing how samples should move. The generator learns to reproduce the flow specified by that field. This shifts the analysis toward the motion induced by training rather than only the divergence named in an objective.

The authors distinguish variational divergence minimization from adversarial training and use that distinction to identify generator losses that can support successful learning. Their analysis suggests additional loss designs may work provided they realize MonoFlow. Empirical studies support the framework’s effectiveness. The resulting contribution is both explanatory and constructive: it offers a different account of GAN dynamics and a condition guiding potential loss designs.
icml-2023-monoflow-rethinking-divergence.tldr: MonoFlow interprets GAN training as learned particle motion, offering a framework for understanding and designing generator losses.

paragraphs: Risk-sensitive reinforcement learning accounts for uncertainty in outcomes when choosing actions over time. Policy-gradient methods have been developed for this purpose, but their global convergence properties are less clear than in risk-neutral settings. This paper investigates those guarantees for a particular class of risk-based objectives.

The authors use Expected Conditional Risk Measures, a class of dynamic, time-consistent risk measures. They derive policy-gradient updates for objectives built from these measures. Their analysis covers both constrained direct policy parameterization and unconstrained softmax parameterization, providing global convergence results and iteration-complexity bounds for the corresponding risk-averse algorithms.

These results connect the choice of risk objective with the behavior of the optimization method used to learn a policy. The authors also test risk-averse versions of REINFORCE and actor-critic algorithms, reporting evidence of effectiveness and the importance of risk control. The theoretical contribution is specific to the ECRM objectives and parameterizations studied; it establishes guarantees for that framework rather than for every possible risk-sensitive reinforcement-learning method.
icml-2023-on-the-global-convergence-of-r.tldr: The paper derives risk-averse policy gradients and proves global convergence for ECRM objectives under two policy parameterizations.

paragraphs: Transferring a reinforcement-learning policy can become difficult when a new environment looks different from the training environment. Many adaptation methods learn a mapping between the two, but require substantial target-domain data or rely heavily on visual similarity. Those strategies can struggle when appearance changes greatly.

Online Prototype Alignment, or OPA, learns the mapping through functional similarity. An exploration mechanism purposefully interacts with unfamiliar elements in the target environment, then connects them to familiar source elements according to what they do. The relevant correspondence comes from the elements’ roles, allowing the framework to pursue policy transfer within only several episodes.

Experiments show that when source and target environments differ visually, OPA achieves better transfer than prior methods while using substantially fewer target samples. The result supports interaction as a way to discover correspondences that appearance alone may obscure. Its significance is the combination of purposeful exploration and functional alignment, which makes limited target-domain experience more useful for adapting an existing policy.
icml-2023-online-prototype-alignment-for.tldr: OPA transfers policies with few target episodes by matching unfamiliar elements to known ones through their functions.

paragraphs: Protein-backbone generation can represent structures through three-dimensional rigid frames, each carrying position and orientation information. Diffusion models operating on such frames had shown promise, but the paper identifies a missing principled framework for diffusion on SE(3), the space of orientation-preserving rigid motions, with the appropriate invariance.

The authors develop theoretical foundations for invariant diffusion over multiple frames and introduce FrameDiff to estimate an equivariant score. These symmetry properties connect the model’s behavior to how structures transform under rigid motion. The framework therefore addresses the geometric foundations of generation as well as providing a method for learning the required score.

Applied to monomer backbone generation, FrameDiff produces designable structures containing up to 500 amino acids without using a pretrained protein-structure prediction network. The authors also find that generated samples can go beyond known protein structures. These findings support FrameDiff as a route to novel, designable backbones while reducing dependence on a pretrained prediction component that had been central to earlier methods.
icml-2023-se-3-diffusion-model-with-appl.tldr: FrameDiff provides a symmetry-aware diffusion framework that generates designable protein backbones up to 500 amino acids.

paragraphs: Seeded graph matching identifies corresponding nodes in two unlabeled graphs using their connectivity and a small set of known matches. Previous neural approaches often require many seeds and do not learn knowledge transferable to new graphs. SeedGNN instead uses supervised training to learn how to match unseen graphs from only a few seeds.

The architecture incorporates two ideas inspired by graph-matching theory. It learns to compute and use witness-like structural evidence from different hop distances in a form that can transfer across graph sizes. It also treats easily matched node pairs as additional seeds, allowing later layers to build on matches established earlier.

Evaluations on synthetic and real-world graphs show substantial improvements over the learning and non-learning methods compared. The experiments also demonstrate transfer from training graphs to test graphs with different sizes and categories. These findings support learning a reusable matching procedure, where structural evidence and progressively expanded seed information work together to identify correspondences beyond the graphs seen during training.
icml-2023-seedgnn-graph-neural-network-f.tldr: SeedGNN learns transferable graph matching from few seeds by combining multi-hop evidence with progressively discovered matches.

paragraphs: A learned environment model can generate imagined experience to supplement an agent’s real observations. Yet value functions also generalize from data, so it is not obvious why learning a separate model should help beyond replaying stored experience. This paper examines when model-based generalization adds useful information.

A theorem motivates how learning a model as an intermediate step can restrict the possible value functions more than directly applying the Bellman equation to observed data. An illustrative neural-network experiment shows a similar effect in a more concrete setting. The proposed benefit therefore concerns the constraints supplied by model learning, not simply the amount of generated experience.

Further online reinforcement-learning experiments study environments with combinatorial complexity and factored structure that a model can generalize over. The authors control other factors as far as possible to isolate benefits over experience replay alone. Their results support model-generated experience in these structured settings, connecting its usefulness to the model’s ability to generalize across the underlying environment.
icml-2023-the-benefits-of-model-based-ge.tldr: Theory and experiments explain how learned environment models can improve reinforcement learning beyond replay through useful structural generalization.
